solution: Wrong. Showing the location of a place is the aim of the ordinary maps studied in earlier classes. Distributional maps are thematic maps, that is, maps prepared with a special theme. Their main aim is to show how a variable such as temperature, rainfall or population is distributed in a region, and such maps easily bring out the patterns of that distribution. Statistical data of the variable is needed to draw them.

Right. In the choropleth method only one value is given to one sub-administrative unit in a region. The value of the variable for the whole unit is taken first, and the unit is then filled with the tint or the pattern of the class in which that value falls. So the whole unit gets a single shade and no change is shown inside it.

Wrong. While making a choropleth map, the smallest and the largest values of the given data are taken into consideration and 5 to 7 classes are made. Each class is assigned a tint of the same colour or a black-and-white pattern. The shades or the patterns become darker with the increasing values of the variable, so the colour changes exactly according to the value of the variable.

Wrong. Altitude is a continuous variable, and when the distribution of a variable is continuous the isopleth method is used, in which places having equal values are joined by lines. The choropleth method is used where the data is available for sub-administrative units and only one value is given to one whole unit. The altitude of the land does not remain the same over a whole taluka or district, so it cannot be shown correctly by the choropleth method.

Wrong. The isopleth method is used when the distribution of a variable is continuous, for example altitude, temperature and rainfall. Population data is gathered by counting, so the distribution of population is shown by the dot method, in which rural population is shown by dots and circles are used for urban population. The density of population, which is one value for each sub-administrative unit, is shown by the choropleth method.

Right. Before a dot map is drawn, the value of a dot has to be determined, for example one dot for 10,000 people. To fix it, the lowest and the highest values of the variable in the region are taken into consideration, and the size of the dot, the density of the variable and the scale of the map are also considered. Only then can the number of dots to be given to each sub-administrative unit be decided. Without a proper value for a dot, the map would need either too many or too few dots and the distribution would not be shown correctly.

Wrong. Isopleth maps are drawn with lines that join locations having the same value, like the contour maps and isobar maps seen in earlier classes. First the class interval is decided by considering the highest and the lowest values of the variable, which fixes the difference between the lines, and then lines are drawn for those intervals. So such lines of equal value are the very basis of an isopleth map.

Right. A dot map is prepared using statistical data gathered through counting, and the dots show the way a variable is distributed throughout the region. Geographical elements such as the population of a region and the distribution of cattle can be shown in this way. The dot method is most suitable for a variable which is freely scattered across the region.

Some maps are prepared with special themes and such maps are called thematic maps. Distributional maps are of this kind: on them the distribution of variables like temperature, rainfall and population is shown according to the data of these variables. They are useful to explain the distribution of these variables in a region, and they easily bring out the patterns of distribution. Statistical data of the variables is needed to draw them. Distribution can be shown on a map in three ways, that is, by the dot method, the choropleth method and the isopleth method.

In the choropleth method the data is shown by shades or tints of various colours or by black-and-white patterns, while in the isopleth method the distribution is shown with the help of lines joining places of equal value. In a choropleth map only one value is given to one sub-administrative unit, whereas in an isopleth map the sub-administrative units are not taken into consideration at all and the data belongs to the respective places, that is, it is point-related data. For a choropleth map the data is obtained through processes such as measurement and surveying, 5 to 7 classes are made, and the shades become darker with increasing values. The isopleth method is used when the distribution of the variable is continuous, such as altitude, temperature or rainfall, and it is assumed that the value changes at a uniform rate between two places. On a choropleth map the change is seen as the shade changes from one unit to the next, while on an isopleth map lines close to each other show a steep change and lines away from each other show a gentle change.

The dot method is the best suited method to show the distribution of population in a region. Population data is gathered through counting, and only such counted data is used while preparing dot maps. The value of a dot is fixed first, for example one dot for 10,000 people, and then the required number of dots is given to each sub-administrative unit, so the actual numbers of people are shown. While placing the dots, the physiography, water sources and the transport system of the region are considered, so the dots fall where people actually live. Rural population is shown by dots and circles are used to show urban population. Since population is freely scattered across a region, this method shows at a glance which parts are densely and which are sparsely populated.

The choropleth method. Wheat production is available taluka by taluka, that is, for each sub-administrative unit, and in this method only one value is given to one sub-administrative unit. Classes are made from the smallest and the largest values of production, and each taluka is given the tint of its class, the shade becoming darker as the production increases.

The isopleth method. The altitude of the land is a continuous variable, and when the distribution of a variable is continuous the isopleth method is used. The altitude of some places in the district is taken as point-related data and the places having the same altitude are joined by lines, so lines close to each other show a steep change in altitude and lines away from each other show a gentle change.

The dot method. Domestic animals are counted, and only data gathered through counting is used while preparing dot maps; the distribution of cattle is itself given in the chapter as an example of this method. Animals are freely scattered across the region, and the dot method is most suitable for such a variable. The value of a dot is decided first, and the required number of dots is then placed in each sub-administrative unit.

The choropleth method. Population density is worked out for each sub-administrative unit, and in this method only one value is given to one such unit. From the smallest and the largest values of the density, 5 to 7 classes are made and each class is given a tint of the same colour or a black-and-white pattern, the shade becoming darker as the density increases. The population density maps of Amravati district in the chapter are drawn in the same way.

The isopleth method. Temperature is a continuous variable, and such distribution is shown by the isopleth method. The accurate temperature of some places in the State is taken as point-related data, the class interval is decided from the highest and the lowest values, and the places having the same temperature are joined by lines. It is assumed that the temperature changes at a uniform rate between two places.

The dot method has been used. The Index of the map shows that each dot stands for 5,000 population, and these dots show the rural population spread over the district. The population of the major cities is shown separately by circles of different sizes, because in the dot method rural population is shown by dots and circles are used to show urban population.

The population is not spread evenly over the district. The dots are packed most closely in the east and the north-east, in Hatkanangale and Shirol, and the middle of the district around Kolhapur (Karvir Taluka) and Panhala is also densely populated; the two circles for the major cities also stand in this central and eastern part. Towards the south and the south-east, in Kagal, Gadhinglaj, Ajra and Chandgad, the dots are fewer and lie further apart, so the population there is moderate. The west and the north-west, that is Shahuwadi, Gaganbavada and Radhanagari, carry very few dots and are the most sparsely populated parts of the district. So the population goes on decreasing from the east and the north-east towards the west and the south-west.

The largest circle is drawn over Kolhapur, which lies in Karvir Taluka in the middle of the district. Compared with the graded circles given in the Index for the population of major cities, it is larger than the Ten Lakhs circle and smaller than the Twenty Lakhs circle, so the map shows the population of Kolhapur as lying between ten lakhs and twenty lakhs.
[Note: the Index supplies only graded circles for Fifty Thousand, One Lakh, Two Lakhs, Five Lakhs, Ten Lakhs and Twenty Lakhs, and no figure is printed beside the circle on the map, so an exact population cannot be read off.]

Gaganbavada Taluka has the least population. It lies in the west of the district, between Shahuwadi to its north and Radhanagari to its south, and only two or three dots are drawn within it, which is by far the smallest number of dots in any taluka of the district. As each dot stands for 5,000 population, this shows that very few people live there. No circle for a major city is drawn in this taluka.
